artboards.title: 8 · Primary vs Promotions — what you can actually control

annotations.text:
CAN IT GO TO PRIMARY?

Short answer: not by configuration, and not reliably for a true broadcast. But there IS one lever, and one design change that helps.

WHAT DOESN'T WORK
There is no header or setting that forces Primary. And the obvious idea — strip the unsubscribe and Feedback-ID headers so it looks less bulky — is actively harmful: Gmail requires them above ~5,000/day, and their absence raises spam-folder risk. Trading Promotions for Spam is a bad deal.

THE DESIGN CHANGE (screen 3)
A message-type switch. "Broadcast" carries the unsubscribe machinery and lands in Promotions. "Operational notice" — seat renewals, account changes, things a recipient needs regardless of preference — is genuinely transactional, carries no unsubscribe, and lands in Primary far more often. The mode is recorded on every send, because dressing marketing up as operational is what gets domains blocked.

THE REAL LEVER
Gmail's tab choice is PER RECIPIENT. If someone replies, stars it, or drags it to Primary, their future mail from suchismita.sen@imotara.com goes to Primary from then on. Asking once, plainly, in the first send is the single most effective thing available — and it costs one sentence.

HONEST CEILING
A genuine broadcast to thousands will mostly sit in Promotions however it is written. That is the inbox, people read it there, and today's test proved it is not spam.

REVISED THIS ROUND

Screen 3 — Compose
· Message-type switch (Broadcast / Operational notice) at the top, because it changes both the headers and the likely inbox tab
· "Likely inbox tab" meter showing what is pushing the message toward Promotions and what is pulling it toward Primary
· Formatting reality kept: fonts limited to stacks that survive Outlook and Gmail, GIF warning for Outlook, Video inserts a poster + link

Screen 7 — Sending status
Now shows the REAL live configuration rather than a how-to: domain verified, SPF/DKIM/DMARC all PASS at Gmail, delivered in 1 second, and the four-week warm-up with week 1 in progress. The send screen refuses anything above the week's ceiling.

Screen 8 — NEW
The full Primary vs Promotions answer.

Unchanged: screens 1, 2, 4, 5, 6.

CONSENT — BUILT INTO THE FLOW

Your list comes from people who approached you. That is a legitimate basis — but GDPR asks you to DEMONSTRATE consent, not merely hold it.

So screen 2 requires provenance before any address can be added:

· Source — one of eight channels
· Free-text detail ("NGO wellbeing day, Salt Lake — stall sign-up sheet")
· Date collected
· Admin who added it

All four are stored per address, shown on the chip, and in the audit export.

NOTE THE WORDING. Every option names something THE PERSON DID — "Emailed us", "Filled in the form on imotara.com", "Messaged or commented on our social media". Not "Website" or "Social media", which quietly stretch to cover an address you found rather than were given. The label is the control; a vague one becomes a laundering route.

Second benefit, not legal: warm contacts complain far less, which protects the domain reputation you are about to spend four weeks warming — and they are far likelier to reply or star, the one thing that actually moves a sender into Gmail's Primary tab.
